title: Triagebox
user: A privacy-conscious person with a messy 1k–10k-file folder who needs to classify it safely without uploading it or letting an opaque tool move files unchecked.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants a local, easy-to-set-up organizer for 1k–10k mixed files; the open-source option crashed and was hard to install.
The asker needs photo organization over an existing SMB/NTFS folder structure, not a tool that takes ownership of the files.

recurrence: Two independent 2025 requests; both stress existing folders, safe operation, and tools that fail at setup or storage compatibility. High pain during cleanup or migration.
current_workaround: Manual folder sorting, Finder/Explorer search, brittle scripts, or moving a copy into a photo server.
incumbents_and_gap: Hazel, DropIt, Local File Organizer, Immich, and PhotoPrism exist; the gap is a transparent, local, review-before-move queue for heterogeneous files that preserves the original tree.
smallest_useful_product: Desktop-local app that inventories one folder, proposes deterministic buckets from filename/type/date/metadata, shows every planned rename/move, executes only approved rows, and writes an undo manifest. Non-goals: cloud sync, generative tagging, or replacing DAM systems.
success_measure: In 10 volunteer folders of at least 1,000 files, users approve or revise 80%+ of proposed actions and can fully undo a run from its manifest.
monetization: one-time — private local cleanup has a clear episodic value and should not require a subscription.
constraints: Process files locally; explicit permission for filesystem access; preserve timestamps and avoid destructive dedupe; make the audit manifest portable JSON/CSV.
why_distinct: It is a reversible file-handoff utility, not an AI auto-organizer: deterministic proposals and an undo receipt are the product.

title: Bookmark Merge Map
user: Someone whose desktop and mobile bookmark trees have diverged and who needs to merge, deduplicate, and find omissions without losing a link.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An HN user has thousands of bookmarks whose manually maintained folders are now difficult to manage and asks for organization plus content search.
A Chrome desktop/mobile user reports months of desync, duplicates, missing bookmarks in same-named folders, and needs a safe re-merge.

recurrence: Two independent 2025 requests describe the same irreversible-risk moment: lots of duplicates and no confidence about what can be removed.
current_workaround: Export HTML, use browser sync and hope it converges, manually compare folders, or switch to Raindrop/xBrowserSync.
incumbents_and_gap: Chrome Sync, Raindrop.io, xBrowserSync, Linkwarden, and Readeck store or sync bookmarks; few make a dry-run reconciliation report across two exported trees the primary job.
smallest_useful_product: Offline browser app that imports two bookmark HTML exports, normalizes canonical URLs, pairs likely duplicates, surfaces conflicts and one-sided links, and exports a merged HTML plus a review CSV. Non-goals: bookmark hosting, AI summaries, and account sync.
success_measure: At least 70% of beta users can produce a merged export with zero unintentionally removed URLs, confirmed by the before/after count report.
monetization: free — a trust-building single-purpose importer is more valuable as a no-account utility and can feed future paid batch features only if requested.
constraints: No network fetch is needed; never overwrite browser data; treat tracking-parameter stripping as a user-reviewable option; preserve original exports.
why_distinct: This is a reconciliation and proof tool before sync, rather than another bookmarking destination.

title: Backup Coverage Ledger
user: A small-team operator who needs to know which critical data sets are covered, by which backup, and whether the backup can actually be extracted.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A team lost production data because critical assets were not tracked; the asker says the hard part is visibility into what needs backup, coverage, and location.
A user switching OS cannot extract files from TrueImage because activation and login infrastructure are unavailable, illustrating that a backup can exist yet be unusable.

recurrence: Two 2025–26 requests show coverage and restoreability—not backup job execution—as the severe failure mode.
current_workaround: Spreadsheets, wiki lists, cron scripts, full-disk snapshots, and periodic manual restore attempts.
incumbents_and_gap: Backblaze, Restic, Borg, Veeam, and cloud snapshots run backups; they do not offer a vendor-neutral, human-readable inventory linking each asset to an owner, retention, extraction method, and restore proof.
smallest_useful_product: Offline/shared YAML-or-CSV ledger with asset records, backup targets, last proof date, recovery instructions, expiry alerts, and a printable restore drill checklist. Non-goals: performing backups or storing credentials.
success_measure: In a pilot of 10 teams, 90% of listed critical assets have an owner, recovery location, and a recorded restore proof within 30 days.
monetization: free — the useful unit is a portable template and validator; no sensitive infrastructure data should be held by the product.
constraints: Local-first data, no secret material, exportable plain files, and clear disclaimer that a record is not a successful restore.
why_distinct: It makes backup coverage auditable across tools instead of becoming another backup engine.

title: Archive Audit
user: A person facing account or device loss who needs an attachment-preserving, locally verifiable archive of messages before access disappears.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN thread asks how people back up their Google accounts, surfacing the need for account-independent preservation.
A WhatsApp Web user who lost their phone fears being logged out after 14 days and losing the only currently accessible message history.

recurrence: Two separate messaging systems in 2025–26 expose the same urgent handoff problem: access is temporary and archives must include attachments and evidence of completeness.
current_workaround: Provider export tools, paid backup utilities, screenshots, forwarding mail, or trusting a device-local cache.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Takeout, Thunderbird, MailStore, and vendor backup tools export data; the unresolved gap is a local audit that tells a non-expert what an archive contains, which attachments are missing, and how it can be reopened later.
smallest_useful_product: Offline inspector for exported MBOX/EML and attachment folders: inventory messages and attachments, flag broken references, hash files, and create an HTML/CSV archive receipt. Non-goals: logging into Gmail/WhatsApp, scraping services, or circumventing platform access controls.
success_measure: For 20 supplied mail exports, the tool identifies attachment-reference mismatches with 100% precision and produces an archive receipt users can open without the app.
monetization: one-time — archival verification is episodic and benefits from an offline trust posture.
constraints: No provider credential handling, all parsing in browser/device, clear format limits, and no promise to export encrypted or proprietary message stores.
why_distinct: It verifies and documents exports people already obtain; it is not a cloud backup service or a platform scraper.

title: Critical Alert Lane
user: An Android user overwhelmed by notifications who needs a tiny offline lane for a few reminders that repeat until explicitly handled.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says notification volume is overwhelming enough to silence the phone, which then buries important events such as a friend's birthday.
A request specifies an offline, no-account calendar whose alerts repeat until manually dismissed and support snoozing and recurrence.

recurrence: Both 2026 requests distinguish urgent, acknowledged reminders from general notification noise; missed reminders are personally consequential.
current_workaround: Turn on Do Not Disturb, add repeated calendar events, rely on default app reminders, or leave the phone on silent.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Calendar, TickTick, Todoist, and Android reminders offer scheduling but mix critical reminders with accounts, feeds, and notification settings; a single acknowledge-or-snooze lane is missing.
smallest_useful_product: Android app with an on-device list of recurring critical reminders, repeat-until-acknowledged behavior, configurable quiet hours, and an export/import file. Non-goals: shared calendars, task management, cloud sync, or AI prioritization.
success_measure: In a 30-day pilot, at least 80% of scheduled critical reminders are acknowledged before their configured escalation window ends.
monetization: one-time — reliability-sensitive personal reminders should remain free of ads and subscriptions.
constraints: Must comply with Android exact-alarm and notification permissions; no contact/calendar permission by default; local encrypted export optional.
why_distinct: It deliberately refuses to be another calendar: acknowledgement reliability is the whole job.

title: Scan Archive Receipt
user: A family historian digitizing albums or rare slides who needs a batch workflow that records provenance, order, and preservation checks before sharing files.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A user has 4,729 digitized family slides with broken chronology and partial labels, wants to share them now, and expects curation to take years.
A user seeks an affordable Android workflow to photograph and enhance books, photo albums, and documents with curved pages.

recurrence: Two 2026 requests show digitization is available but the handoff from scans to a durable, intelligible collection remains laborious.
current_workaround: Phone scanning apps, ad hoc folders, filenames, cloud albums, Internet Archive upload, and a separate spreadsheet.
incumbents_and_gap: Google PhotoScan, Adobe Scan, Microsoft Lens, and Internet Archive handle capture or hosting; none creates a lightweight batch provenance sheet tying scans to physical source, order, rights, and checksums.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA that imports a scan batch, records source item/page/order/date/rights notes, generates stable filenames and checksums, and exports a CSV plus HTML contact sheet. Non-goals: OCR, image enhancement, cloud hosting, or historical identification.
success_measure: Users can take a 100-image batch from import to a complete metadata/checksum receipt in under 20 minutes without creating a separate spreadsheet.
monetization: one-time — archival projects are finite and require durable offline exports.
constraints: Never alter originals; EXIF may be sensitive; metadata exports must be UTF-8 and interoperable; rights fields are descriptive, not legal advice.
why_distinct: It is preservation bookkeeping around scans, not another scanner or photo gallery.

title: Large Type Catalog
user: A low-vision knowledge worker or older family member who needs to inspect and sort a local photo collection with reliably large controls and keyboard/voice-friendly operations.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A knowledge worker with declining vision says modern browser apps lack usable keybindings and asks how to prepare for low vision.
A vacation-photo owner needs semi-duplicate removal, multi-dimensional batch tagging, templated renaming, notes, and a multifaceted display.

recurrence: The 2025 accessibility request and 2026 photo-management request overlap on high-volume visual classification where dense, mouse-first interfaces fail.
current_workaround: Apple Photos/Google Photos, Explorer/Finder, small thumbnails, or a full DAM with many inaccessible controls.
incumbents_and_gap: Apple Photos, digiKam, Immich, and PhotoPrism are feature-rich; the gap is an intentionally low-vision-first, local triage surface with oversized actions and simple keyboard sequencing.
smallest_useful_product: Local browser catalog for one folder: huge thumbnails, adjustable contrast and text, keyboard-only keep/reject/tag/rename queue, and CSV sidecar export. Non-goals: face recognition, cloud gallery, image editing, or replacing a DAM.
success_measure: Five low-vision testers can complete a 50-photo keep/tag/rename exercise with keyboard only and rate all primary controls readable at their preferred scale.
monetization: free — accessibility utility adoption depends on zero-friction local access; optional paid packaged desktop version can follow validation.
constraints: Meet WCAG 2.2 AA where applicable; semantic controls and no color-only state; local files must not be uploaded; support reduced motion.
why_distinct: The differentiator is accessible classification workflow, not AI photo organization or a general gallery.

title: CSV Keyed Diff
user: An implementation or operations worker who must compare two customer CSV exports by business key and explain row/column changes without a database or spreadsheet gymnastics.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A software implementation worker calls cleaning and mapping legacy CSV/XLSX exports for import a constant pain and asks for practical workarounds.
The asker needs a portable, gratis CSV comparison that highlights differing row/columns; line-by-line diff breaks when rows are added or removed.

recurrence: Two 2025 business-data requests independently reject plain text diff because records move and the useful unit is a changed field by key.
current_workaround: VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP, conditional formatting, text diff, Power Query, or ad hoc scripts.
incumbents_and_gap: Excel, LibreOffice, Beyond Compare, csvkit, and Data Wrangler help, but setup is high and generic diff does not force a reviewable business-key comparison report.
smallest_useful_product: Offline web app that accepts two CSVs, lets users choose one or more key columns, detects adds/removes/field changes, resolves duplicate keys, and exports a filtered change report. Non-goals: database connectors, cleansing automation, or cloud storage.
success_measure: For a seeded 10k-row fixture with inserts, deletes, reorders, and updates, results match the expected keyed changes with 100% recall and users identify the chosen key in under two minutes.
monetization: one-time — data may be confidential and comparison is an occasional high-value task.
constraints: All files stay local; handle UTF-8/quoted cells/large files; disclose duplicate-key ambiguity; make no inference from sensitive data.
why_distinct: It is a reconciliation report generator, not a spreadsheet, generic diff viewer, or LLM data-cleaning wrapper.

title: Table Lens
user: A developer or analyst who needs to inspect an unfamiliar CSV/TSV safely and quickly without ads, uploads, broken columns, or launching a spreadsheet.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The author describes existing free CSV viewers as ad-heavy, unclear, and slow, and asks what people use to view or convert CSV files.
A user asks for a command-line CSV viewer like less that spaces columns correctly on Linux or macOS.

recurrence: Two February 2026 requests converge on a basic unmet need: fast, legible, trustworthy tabular inspection rather than analysis.
current_workaround: Excel/LibreOffice, online upload viewers, less/cat, csvlook, or a one-off script.
incumbents_and_gap: csvlook, xsv, Miller, VS Code extensions, and web viewers exist; the gap is an offline, zero-install lens with robust delimiter/encoding inference and a shareable inspection receipt.
smallest_useful_product: PWA that opens CSV/TSV locally, detects delimiter/encoding/header, supports frozen columns, type hints, filter/search, and exports a small schema/profile report. Non-goals: editing, database querying, charts, or data upload.
success_measure: On a 100-file corpus of common CSV/TSV variants, the app renders the correct column count without manual settings for 95%+ of files.
monetization: free — inspection utilities gain adoption through no-account trust; a later CLI companion can be paid only if demand is proven.
constraints: Local file processing, memory limits for large files, explicit encoding confidence, and accessibility support for keyboard table navigation.
why_distinct: It deliberately stops at trustworthy inspection and a portable profile, avoiding the crowded spreadsheet/BI category.

title: Review Packet
user: A professional handing an internally reviewed document to an external reviewer who needs comments, change context, and attachments visible without giving access to the source workspace.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker lists exporting Notion to Docs/Word, re-attaching PDFs, and copy-pasting decisions among tools as repeated workflow friction.
An Overleaf user needs comments and tracked changes made visible to external parties who only receive the exported PDF.

recurrence: Two 2025–26 requests show that an exported PDF is not a sufficient review handoff when context and comments stay in the originating tool.
current_workaround: Screenshots, copy/paste into an email, Word tracked changes, separate attachment lists, or giving reviewers unwanted workspace access.
incumbents_and_gap: Adobe Acrobat, Overleaf, Notion, Google Docs, and Word support pieces of review; the gap is a simple neutral packet that carries a document plus decision/comment context across tools.
smallest_useful_product: Static local packet builder: add a PDF, structured comments/decisions, source links, and attachments; export a self-contained HTML folder and print stylesheet. Non-goals: editing PDFs, OCR, collaboration accounts, or conversion from proprietary workspaces.
success_measure: In a usability test, 8 of 10 external reviewers can locate every requested comment, decision, and attachment without signing in or asking the sender for context.
monetization: one-time — a document-handoff utility is event-based and must work offline for sensitive review packets.
constraints: Do not embed third-party document content without user authority; warn about sensitive data in exported folders; no claims of legal record retention.
why_distinct: It is a cross-tool review handoff artifact, not yet another PDF editor or generic document converter.

title: Photo Intake Receipt
user: A person moving phone photos to a PC who needs a resilient transfer record: which files arrived, which did not, and which can be safely deleted from the phone.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A cross-platform transfer builder says common options remain constrained by platforms, size limits, folders, network interruptions, and restart-on-failure behavior.
An Android-to-Windows user reports transfers hanging for more than four minutes for 400 MB despite trying multiple USB cables and hubs.

recurrence: Two late-2025 sources describe transfer as still unreliable across devices; the risk is not just speed but believing an incomplete transfer succeeded.
current_workaround: USB cables, cloud drives, AirDrop-like tools, WeTransfer, retrying transfers, and manually eyeballing file counts.
incumbents_and_gap: LocalSend, KDE Connect, AirDroid, Syncthing, Zynk, and cloud drives move files; the gap is a deliberately narrow intake receipt that compares a selected phone batch to the destination before deletion.
smallest_useful_product: Companion desktop/Android pair that transfers a selected batch on LAN, resumes chunks, hashes files, and creates a signed-style receipt listing source count, destination count, missing files, and safe-to-delete status. Non-goals: general chat, remote cloud sharing, media management, or an account service.
success_measure: Under forced Wi-Fi interruption in 20 test transfers, every completed receipt correctly identifies all missing or changed files and resumed transfers avoid re-sending 90%+ of completed bytes.
monetization: one-time — this is a reliability appliance, not a storage subscription.
constraints: Use local-network permissions only, encrypt transport, preserve EXIF, respect Android storage restrictions, and be explicit that a receipt is only as good as the selected source set.
why_distinct: The product is the verifiable intake/deletion decision, not another broad file-transfer clone.

title: Ledger Import Check
user: A privacy-sensitive household or freelancer who keeps finances locally and needs to import a bank CSV, detect duplicates, and reconcile an opening/closing balance without giving a budgeting app account access.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A localStorage/IndexedDB budgeting-tool builder asks about multi-year history, backup/sync, and whether people trust browser storage for financial records.
A user maintaining a Dropbox CSV spreadsheet needs a free format editable on Windows, Linux, and Android without sacrificing spreadsheet functionality.

recurrence: These 2025 requests show continuing demand for portable, private personal records, alongside uncertainty about storage durability and cross-device handoff.
current_workaround: Spreadsheets, bank portals, commercial budgeting apps, manual CSV cleanup, and copies in cloud storage.
incumbents_and_gap: YNAB, Actual Budget, GnuCash, Firefly III, and spreadsheets cover budgeting; the gap is a small local import/reconciliation checkpoint that can feed any ledger format and produce an evidence report.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA that maps a bank CSV, fingerprints potential duplicates, checks running balances against supplied opening/closing values, flags unexplained gaps, and exports cleaned CSV plus a reconciliation receipt. Non-goals: Plaid, investment advice, tax filing, budgeting philosophy, or cloud sync.
success_measure: On a seeded 12-month statement corpus, the tool detects 100% of injected duplicate/missing transactions and users reconcile a monthly import in under 10 minutes.
monetization: one-time — financial privacy and no-account operation are core to the value proposition.
constraints: No server upload or credentials; encrypt-at-rest only when the platform supports it; disclose browser-storage limits; never offer financial advice or tax calculations.
why_distinct: It is a neutral reconciliation gate before a ledger, not another subscription budgeting app.
